theme-a-molecules-and-cells: Why does salt vanish into water while oil sits on top in a separate layer?
How can weak attractions between molecules hold up an insect and keep a lake's temperature steady?
How does water reach the top of the tallest tree with no pump and no energy spent by the tree?
Why does a plant lose water fastest on a warm, dry, windy day, and how can you measure it?
DNA's two strands are held together only by weak bonds. So why doesn't the molecule fall apart?
theme-a-organisms-and-ecosystems: Cuttings from one plant share every gene. So why don't they all grow to the same height?
If two groups of the same animal never meet again, how do they end up as different species?
How can just two words tell you where any living thing fits among millions?
Why are some microbes that look just like bacteria placed further from them than you are from a mushroom?
The first human genome took years and a fortune to read. What can we do now that it is quick and cheap?
Two meadows hold exactly the same species. How can one of them be far more diverse than the other?
Why can a whole field of crop plants be wiped out by a single new disease?
theme-b-molecules-and-cells: Glucose and fructose are built from exactly the same atoms. So what makes them different sugars?
Starch and cellulose are both chains of glucose. Why can one feed you while the other builds a tree?
A cell's outer membrane is just two molecules thick. Why do its molecules form that sheet by themselves?
How can you show that the molecules in a membrane never stop moving?
Cross a red flower with a white one and every offspring is pink. So why do red and white come back?
theme-b-organisms-and-ecosystems: Why can an amoeba survive without lungs or a heart, but you can't?
What do lungs, gills and leaves have in common that makes them so good at swapping gases?
How does a leaf take in the gas it needs without drying out?
Two sets of results share the same average but look nothing alike. What number captures the difference?
Two bars on a graph have different heights. When does that difference actually mean something?
Blood leaves the heart in surges but creeps past your cells in a steady trickle. How?
theme-c-metabolism-respiration-photosynt: How can a protein make a reaction millions of times faster, yet come out of it unchanged?
Is an enzyme a rigid lock waiting for one key, or does it change shape as its target arrives?
Why does warming an enzyme speed it up, until suddenly it hardly works at all?
Plants given a new fertiliser grew taller, but they also sat nearest the window. Can you trust the result?
Your core temperature barely moves in snow or in sun. How does your body manage that, and at what cost?
Burning sugar releases all its energy in one flash. How do your cells release it slowly enough to use?
How can a drug that once cured an infection stop working against the very same germ?
theme-c-signalling-and-body-systems: Your body temperature wobbles all day. Why is that a sign that control is working, not failing?
You eat a sugary snack, yet your blood sugar barely changes for long. What pulls it back?
Two people both have high blood sugar, but only one lacks insulin. How can that be?
Why is an egg released in the middle of the cycle, and not at the start or the end?
Your brain has separate parts with separate jobs. So how do they add up to one thinking mind?
theme-d-molecules-and-cells: How can a speck of DNA from one hair be copied into billions and then sorted by size?
If almost all human DNA is shared, how can a trace of it point to just one person?
A ribosome never sees a single amino acid's name. So how does it build the right protein?
Change one letter in a gene: does the protein always change?
theme-d-organisms-and-ecosystems: Most flowers have both male and female parts. Why do so many work hard to avoid pollinating themselves?
A dry bean can sit in a jar for years, then sprout within days of getting wet. What powers that first growth?
Two tall pea plants can produce a short one. Where was the short plant hiding?
Why do some inherited conditions turn up far more often in sons than in daughters?
Why doesn't selection always push a population in the same direction?
If people clear part of a rainforest, could the rest of it dry out and die?
a1-molecules-part-2: DNA uses just four kinds of base. How can that be enough to hold the instructions for a whole organism?
A bacterium has no nucleus. So where does it keep its genes, and what else does it manage without?
Every time your cells build a big molecule, they make water. Why?
Before a cell divides, it copies all of its DNA. How does the copy come out almost perfect?
How did one experiment with heavy nitrogen show that every new DNA molecule keeps half of the old one?
a1-molecules-part-3: DNA has only four letters. How can a gene spell out a protein built from twenty different building blocks?
Two animals look almost identical. How can biologists tell whether they are truly close relatives?
How can we trust the evidence that living things have changed over time?
Stretched out, the DNA in one of your cells would be taller than you. How does it fit inside the nucleus?
Your body cells carry chromosomes in pairs. How can you tell which two belong together?
a2-cells: Oily molecules avoid water, yet they wrap every cell in a thin film. How does that film build itself?
How can you measure the length of a cell you can only see through a microscope?
If you can enlarge an image as much as you like, why do some things inside a cell stay blurred?
An electron microscope shows a cell packed with odd shapes. How do you tell what each one is and does?
A plant cell shares most of its parts with yours. So what does it have that yours lacks, and why?
Your nerve cells and muscle cells carry the same genes. So why are they so different?
A single cell can feed, move and reproduce on its own. So why are so many living things made of many cells?
a2-cells-part-2: Some of your cells have no nucleus and some have hundreds. How does a cell's build match its job?
Why does a good biology drawing leave out most of what you can see down the microscope?
Nearly every cell in your body carries the same genes. So why doesn't a skin cell act like a nerve cell?
How does one virus turn the body's own defenders into factories that make more of it?
If no animal can change its own genes, how can a whole population change over time?
Nobody designs a drug-resistant germ, so how do whole populations of them appear so quickly?
a4-ecosystems: A desert fox has enormous ears and almost never drinks. How did it end up so well suited to the desert?
One extra chromosome can change a whole body. So how do some plants thrive with doubled sets?
Species have always gone extinct. So why are biologists so alarmed by the extinctions happening now?
If the last of a species survives safely in a zoo, has that species really been saved?
How can people keep taking food and materials from nature without wrecking it?
b1-molecules-part-2: Why is butter solid but olive oil runny, when both are made of the same kind of molecule?
Hormones reach almost every cell in the body. So why does each one affect only a few?
Every protein in your body is built from just twenty building blocks. How can so few make so many?
A protein is only a chain of amino acids. So how does it fold into the exact shape its job needs?
b2-cells: Oxygen slips straight through a cell membrane, yet a smaller sodium ion is stopped. Why?
Why would a drip of pure water into a patient's vein do harm?
Potato pieces gain mass in some sugar solutions and lose it in others. What does the point in between reveal?
A cell keeps taking in a substance it already holds more of than its surroundings. How is that possible?
Why does a resting nerve cell keep spending energy when it is not sending any signal?
Why do some nerve signals race faster than a car while others creep along at walking pace?
A nerve signal reaches a gap it cannot jump. So how does the message get across?
b2-cells-part-2: Food in your gut is still outside your body. So when does a meal actually get inside you?
To study one part of a cell, you first have to smash the cell open. How do you get that part out undamaged?
Your DNA never leaves the nucleus. So how do its instructions reach the place where proteins are made?
A plant takes in carbon dioxide and water and gives out oxygen. Which of the two did the oxygen come from?
A green leaf also hides orange and yellow pigments. How can you reveal them, and what are they for?
Your body makes about four million new cells a second. How does each one get a full set of chromosomes?
A microscope slide freezes a root tip in one instant. How can counting its cells reveal time?
b2-cells-part-3: An early embryo is a ball of identical cells. How does it know where to build a head and a tail?
One early embryo cell can grow into a whole baby. Why can't a cell from your bone marrow?
Why are almost all cells too small to see, even inside the largest animals?
How do your lungs pull air in when they have no muscle of their own?
How can you tell from the outside how well a person's lungs are working?
An egg is a giant cell and a sperm is a tiny one. Why are the two cells built so differently?
Meiosis in a testis gives four sperm, but meiosis in an ovary gives just one egg. Why?
b3-organisms-part-2: How can a fatty streak inside an artery wall end in a heart attack years later?
Countries that eat more fat have more heart disease. Does that prove the fat is the cause?
A difference between two groups could be real or just luck. How do biologists decide which?
How does water get from the soil into a root, and how do desert plants keep hold of it?
Cut every nerve to a heart and it keeps on beating. So what are those nerves for?
b4-ecosystems: A rock pool and a rainforest are both called ecosystems. What do they have in common?
Two kinds of barnacle can both live low on the shore. Why is only one of them ever found there?
How can you know how many snails live in a whole wood without finding every single one?
Why do places on opposite sides of the world, with no link between them, end up looking so alike?
Some bacteria thrive in total darkness with no food, just dissolved iron and gases. How do they grow?
A fungus has no mouth and no stomach. So how does it digest a fallen tree?
A skull is all that is left of an animal. How can its teeth reveal what it ate?
b4-ecosystems-part-2: When oxygen runs out, muscles make lactate and yeast makes alcohol. What do they gain from it?
Energy flows along every food chain but never comes back. So where does it start, and where does it go?
A caterpillar eats a whole leaf. Why does so little of that leaf end up as caterpillar?
Why are top predators so rare, and why does eating lower in a food chain feed more people?
Why does a population that doubles again and again eventually stop growing?
Why do members of the same species often compete harder with each other than with any other species?
How can losing a few otters turn a forest of seaweed into bare rock?
c1-molecules-part-2: Your cells already get energy from sugar. Why do they spend it through a different molecule first?
How can a bead of liquid creeping along a thin tube show how fast seeds respire, and which fuel they use?
One spot of a mixture goes in; a ladder of spots comes out. How do you work out what each spot is?
Brighter lamps stop making a greenhouse crop grow any faster. What should the grower change instead?
The carbon atoms in your body were once in the air. How do they keep being recycled?
Every year the air's carbon dioxide rises and falls, yet it keeps on climbing. What drives both patterns?
Why can a warming of just a degree or two force species to move, or vanish from a place?
c3-c4-organisms-and-ecosystems: Why does your hand jerk away from a hot pan before you have even felt the pain?
Your heart races and your pupils widen before you have decided anything. So who gave the order?
Your body carries trillions of microbes, yet very few make you ill. What makes something a pathogen?
Most germs that land on you never get in, and most that do never get far. What stops them?
Blood must flow freely through every vessel, yet seal a cut within minutes. How does it do both?
c3-c4-organisms-and-ecosystems-part-2: Your body has never met this year's flu virus, yet it makes antibodies that fit it. How?
A second infection with the same virus often passes without you noticing. What changed inside you?
Some vaccines protect for life, but the flu vaccine changes every year. Why the difference?
Nearly four-fifths of the air is nitrogen. So why do crops so often run short of it?
d1-d2-molecules-and-cells-part-2: Can a living thing ever mutate because it needs to?
Many cells in your body could still divide, yet most of the time they hold back. What keeps them in check?
Each parent passes on chromosomes, yet the number never doubles. How is it halved so exactly?
Brothers and sisters share both parents, yet each gets a different genetic mix. Where does it come from?
